paragraphs.text: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-89 (DEE89) is an autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder. Seizures begin in the neonatal or early infantile period and are often epileptic spasms or myoclonic seizures. Early EEG often shows a suppression-burst pattern or hypsarrhythmia. Affected individuals have severe to profound developmental delay and intellectual disability with abnormal muscle tone. Some patients also have non-neural features, including cleft palate, omphalocele, joint contractures, pes equinovarus, scoliosis, and dysmorphic facial features (Chatron et al., 2020; Neuray et al., 2020).

paragraphs.text: Chatron et al. (2020) reported 11 patients from 6 unrelated consanguineous families of Algerian, Egyptian, Turkish (2 families), Iranian, and Brazilian origin. Seizures began in the first 2 months of life in all patients. All 10 patients with available early history had seizure onset in the first month of life. Seizures at onset were mainly epileptic spasms (6 patients) or myoclonic seizures (5 patients). Seven of 8 patients with EEG recordings in the neonatal period had a suppression-burst pattern or a variant with interburst attenuation. Two patients whose first EEG was recorded later had hypsarrhythmia. Six patients eventually achieved seizure control with antiepileptic drugs. All living patients had severe psychomotor delay, and intellectual disability was profound in all who could be assessed. Neurologic features included axial hypotonia, spasticity, tetraparesis, dystonia, and hyperkinetic movements. Head circumference was normal in all but 1 patient. Brain MRI was normal in 5 patients. Abnormal findings included hypoplastic corpus callosum with dilated subarachnoid spaces and progressive cerebral and cerebellar atrophy in 1 patient, and mild cerebral atrophy with ventricular enlargement at age 6 years in another patient. Seven patients had cleft palate, 6 had joint contractures, 5 had pes equinovarus, and 4 had scoliosis. Two sibs had omphalocele, and 3 patients had facial dysmorphic features without clear common elements. Four patients died before 4 years of age. One of these, born at 29 weeks' gestation, died at 9 days of age.

paragraphs.text: Among the patients reported by Chatron et al. (2020), the affected Egyptian sibs (Family B) had additional congenital anomalies. paragraphs.text: Neuray et al. (2020) reported 6 patients from 6 unrelated families of Persian, Pakistani, African American, Sudanese, Egyptian, and Turkish ancestry. In the text, 4 patients were stated to be born to consanguineous parents. All were born at term after a normal pregnancy. Seizures began between 2 and 6 months of age and were mainly focal motor seizures with or without impaired awareness. Two patients had epileptic spasms, 4 had focal non-motor seizures, and 5 had bilateral motor seizures. Seizures were pharmacologically controlled in 3 patients and drug-resistant in 3. EEG at onset showed burst suppression in 2 patients, diffuse slowing with multifocal and generalized sharp waves in 2, and hypsarrhythmia in 2. Cranial MRI was normal in all but 2 patients: 1 had slight ventricular enlargement and 1 had moderate global atrophy. All patients had severe developmental delay, and most did not achieve speech. One patient developed simple speech, had moderate intellectual disability, and remained seizure-free on medication. Five patients had reduced muscle strength. Four were unable to sit or crawl or had limited head control, and 2 depended on a nasogastric tube because of dysphagia. Four patients had slight dysmorphic facial features, and only 1 had cleft palate. That patient also had congenital bilateral hip dislocation with shallow acetabulum, talipes equinovarus, and hearing impairment. Other features without clear common elements included hirsutism, kidney stones, urogenital malformations, diastasis recti, reduced head circumference, clinodactyly, short arms, and arthrogryposis of the lower limbs. Metabolic workups were normal.

paragraphs.text: Chatron et al. (2020) studied 11 patients from 6 consanguineous families with DEE89 using whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing. Every affected individual carried a homozygous GAD1 variant, and in each case this was the only likely pathogenic variant retained after filtering. Sanger sequencing confirmed segregation with the disease in all families. Four families carried truncating variants. These were a splice site mutation (c.1414-1G-C) and a 5-bp deletion causing a frameshift (c.812_816delTTAAG). The fourth truncating variant was the nonsense mutation R531X, which was shared by an Iranian family and a Turkish family. cDNA analysis of the splice site mutation showed no normal mRNA product and 3 aberrant isoforms. In an Egyptian family, the authors found an in-frame 3-bp deletion (c.695_697delAGA; K232del). In a cell-free assay, the mutant protein was expressed at a level comparable to wildtype. In a Brazilian family, they found a missense mutation (E509K) in the pyridoxal-dependent decarboxylase domain. Structural modeling predicted that this change would disrupt salt bridges.

His sister, who carried the variant in the heterozygous state, had a different neurodevelopmental condition without seizures.
